paragraphs: Contract design asks how a principal should pay for outcomes when those payments influence an agent's actions. The difficulty is that changing a contract can change which action the agent chooses, producing abrupt changes in the principal's utility. This paper introduces a deep learning approach that explicitly represents that discontinuous structure.

Its Discontinuous ReLU network, or DeLU, describes utility using separate affine pieces, each corresponding to a particular agent action. The network implicitly learns both the conditions under which an action serves the agent's interests and the principal's utility objective. These learned pieces support parallel optimization through linear programming or interior-point methods.

This representation connects learning a utility function with searching for a good contract: the learned structure can be used directly in optimization. The reported experiments show that DeLU approximates utility with relatively few training samples and scales to problems containing many actions and outcomes. The resulting contracts are approximately optimal, making the empirical contribution one of scalable approximation rather than an unconditional claim of exact recovery.
neurips-2023-deep-contract-design-via-di.tldr: DeLU networks represent discontinuous contract utilities and support scalable searches for approximately optimal contracts.

paragraphs: Novelty detection identifies observations that look unusual relative to familiar data. Conformal inference can calibrate a machine learning detector without specifying a particular data distribution, but its randomization can produce different findings when the same data are analyzed again. This instability makes it harder to interpret which discoveries deserve attention.

The paper replaces conformal p-values with suitable conformal e-values as measures of statistical evidence. This allows evidence from repeated analyses of the same data to be combined while retaining a proof of false discovery rate control. That control concerns the expected proportion of false discoveries among the observations flagged as novel.

The method also weights e-values using additional information carefully extracted from the same data. The authors show that randomness can be reduced without much loss of detection power, partly because of this weighting. Experiments with synthetic and real data support the approach's ability to remove random variation in findings, and sometimes show greater power. The benefit is more stable detection with a statistical error guarantee, rather than a promise that every individual detection is correct.
neurips-2023-derandomized-novelty-detect.tldr: Combining conformal e-values makes novelty detection more stable while provably controlling the false discovery rate.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks communicate through patterns of discrete spikes, carrying information through both spike counts and spike timing. Time-based training aims to exploit timing information and support asynchronous learning. Yet some methods using this training strategy rely on losses dominated by spike counts, raising a question about how the training scheme and loss fit together.

The paper maps rate-based losses to time-based counterparts and explains why they can still work within time-based training. Its theoretical analysis suggests that losses supplying adequate positive overall gradients help learning. Guided by that analysis, the authors introduce an enhanced counting loss to replace the commonly used mean square counting loss.

The approach also transfers learning of the scale factor in weight standardization into the firing thresholds. Experiments show better performance than previous time-based training methods on most evaluated datasets. The contribution therefore includes both a practical training modification and an explanation of how count-based objectives relate to temporal learning. The reported advantage applies to most datasets tested, rather than establishing that the proposed loss is universally superior.
neurips-2023-exploring-loss-functions-fo.tldr: An analysis of gradients motivates an enhanced counting loss that improves time-based spiking-network training on most evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: Continual semantic segmentation requires a model to learn new image classes while retaining its ability to recognize earlier ones. This paper adds a fairness objective to that process through a framework based on class distributions. Its focus connects fairness with how the segmentation model learns across classes as its knowledge expands.

The method introduces a Prototypical Contrastive Clustering loss to address catastrophic forgetting and background shift. These challenges arise when learning new classes disrupts earlier knowledge and when what counts as background changes during continual learning. The authors also prove that their loss provides a generalized form of knowledge distillation, a commonly used way to transfer or retain learned information.

A second component, Conditional Structural Consistency loss, regularizes the structure of the predicted segmentation. Together, these components address preservation of class knowledge and consistency of the spatial predictions. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on ADE20K, Cityscapes, and Pascal VOC, alongside improved segmentation fairness. These findings support treating class-distribution fairness as part of the continual learning objective while also pursuing strong scene-understanding performance.
neurips-2023-fairness-continual-learning.tldr: A class-distribution-based fairness framework combines new losses to improve continual segmentation, knowledge retention, and fairness.

paragraphs: Quadrature approximates an integral by evaluating a function at selected locations and combining those values. Kernel quadrature uses a kernel-defined function space to guide this approximation. The paper studies functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, where choosing useful evaluation locations is central to obtaining accurate integration without an expensive computational procedure.

The authors construct new quadrature rules whose evaluation locations, or nodes, come from randomly pivoted Cholesky sampling. This addresses a tradeoff identified in earlier kernel quadrature methods: some offer limited accuracy, while others depend on sampling problems that are difficult to solve efficiently. The proposed sampling procedure offers a practical route to selecting nodes.

Theoretical and numerical results show that the method is fast and reaches quadrature error rates comparable to more expensive approaches using continuous volume sampling, thinning, and recombination. The authors also emphasize that it adapts readily to complicated geometries and arbitrary kernels. Its significance is the combination of competitive integration accuracy and a simpler computational path to constructing the quadrature rule.
neurips-2023-kernel-quadrature-with-rand.tldr: Randomly pivoted Cholesky sampling builds fast kernel quadrature rules with error rates comparable to more computationally expensive methods.

paragraphs: Sampling in a constrained domain means generating samples while respecting restrictions on where those samples can lie. The paper introduces particle-based algorithms for this task that do not require a learning rate. This removes a tuning choice that otherwise affects how a sampling procedure progresses toward its target distribution.

The approach combines coin-betting ideas from convex optimization with a view of constrained sampling as mirrored optimization over probability measures. In that view, optimization operates on distributions while accounting for the domain's constraints. The authors also use this perspective to build a common framework for existing methods, including mirrored Langevin dynamics and mirrored Stein variational gradient descent.

Numerical examples cover targets on the simplex, fairness-constrained sampling, and constrained problems arising in post-selection inference. Across these examples, the results indicate performance competitive with existing constrained samplers without hyperparameter tuning. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and conceptual: it offers sampling methods that reduce tuning effort and a shared formulation that relates several approaches to the same underlying optimization viewpoint.
neurips-2023-learning-rate-free-sampling.tldr: Coin-betting-based particle samplers handle constrained domains without learning-rate tuning and show competitive numerical performance.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning asks a model to adapt to a task using only a small number of labeled examples. Meta-learning helps by transferring knowledge learned across tasks. This paper focuses on the adaptation procedure itself, arguing that learning a good initialization or learning rate can leave useful information from earlier weight updates underused.

Meta-AdaM learns an adaptive optimizer that takes weight-update history as input when predicting learning rates. This gives the update rule access to how optimization has been progressing, rather than relying only on a task's starting point. The method also incorporates momentum through a double look-ahead mechanism, with the aim of accelerating convergence in the few-shot setting.

The authors report extensive benchmark experiments supporting Meta-AdaM's effectiveness. The central contribution is to combine a history-aware learning-rate learner with momentum within meta-learned adaptation. This matters because limited labeled data makes the behavior of each adaptation step especially relevant. The paper presents the combined optimizer as a way to obtain rapid convergence, drawing on optimization behavior that has been useful in settings with many labeled examples.
neurips-2023-meta-adam-an-meta-learned-a.tldr: Meta-AdaM combines history-informed learning rates and momentum to accelerate adaptation in few-shot learning.

paragraphs: Classification tasks arriving over time often evolve gradually, so neighboring tasks can be more similar than distant ones. This creates an opportunity to share information when each task has few examples. The paper considers learning across the whole sequence, including using earlier tasks to help later ones and later tasks to improve earlier ones.

The authors introduce incremental minimax risk classifiers, or IMRCs, that account for this evolving relationship while supporting both forward and backward learning. This addresses a gap in approaches designed around similarities that do not depend on time, as well as methods focused solely on the most recent task. The objective includes improving classification throughout the growing sequence.

The theoretical analysis characterizes performance gains in terms of the number of tasks and their expected quadratic change, a measure of how tasks evolve. Experiments show that IMRCs can substantially improve performance, particularly when sample sizes are small. Together, these results connect the value of information sharing to the amount of task evolution and show why revisiting earlier tasks can be useful.
neurips-2023-minimax-forward-and-backwar.tldr: Incremental minimax classifiers exploit both earlier and later evolving tasks, with theoretical performance characterizations and strong small-sample results.

paragraphs: Neural Priming adapts a large pretrained model when a new task or data distribution offers few or no labeled examples. Its starting point is that pretraining may already contain relevant material. Given class names or unlabeled test samples, the method recalls relevant pretraining data and conditions the model's parameters on that data.

The recalled examples support lightweight updates that prepare the model for the target distribution. The authors report that this process can run at test time even with a pretraining dataset as large as LAION-2B. The approach therefore uses the new task's available cues to make earlier training experience useful for adaptation.

Experiments report accuracy improvements across distribution-shift and transfer-learning benchmarks. In zero-shot evaluation, the stated improvements are 2.45% on ImageNet and 3.81% on average across standard transfer benchmarks. A test-time inference scheme also improves ImageNetV2 accuracy by 1.41%. These findings support recalling and updating on relevant pretraining data as a way to adapt under limited labeling and changing distributions.
neurips-2023-neural-priming-for-sample-e.tldr: Neural Priming recalls relevant pretraining data and uses lightweight updates to improve adaptation with few or no labeled examples.

paragraphs: In a partially observable environment, an agent must choose actions without directly seeing all the information that matters. A recurrent policy can help by maintaining a compact context drawn from past transitions. This paper asks how that context can capture more information about the environment's dynamics, rather than relying only on the current observation.

The proposed approach combines an ordinary differential equation-based recurrent model with model-free reinforcement learning. The recurrent component uses historical information to help infer what is hidden, while the ODE formulation provides a way to represent evolution over time. The aim is to make the policy's internal context more informative about dynamics in partially observable decision problems.

Experiments demonstrate effectiveness across partially observable continuous-control and meta-reinforcement-learning tasks. They also show robustness when observations arrive irregularly, which the authors attribute to the ability of ODEs to handle irregularly sampled time series. This connects the representation choice to a concrete observation challenge: useful temporal context must account for how observations are distributed over time.
neurips-2023-ode-based-recurrent-model-f.tldr: An ODE-based recurrent model improves temporal context for model-free reinforcement learning under partial and irregular observation.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from previously collected data, but deployment may hide information that was available during training. A policy trained with complete observations can then become unreliable. The challenge is greater when the particular observation components that will be missing are unknown in advance.

ORDER addresses this problem through discrete state representations and proxy representations inferred from partially observed trajectories. Training first learns discrete representations from fully observed data, then trains a decision module using those representations. A third stage learns proxy representations from data with varied partial observations, aligning them with the representations obtained from complete observations.

The alignment gives the decision module a common representational target even when its available observations change. Experiments across diverse partially observable scenarios demonstrate the framework's effectiveness and highlight the role of discrete proxies in generalization. ORDER is designed to accommodate different offline reinforcement learning algorithms. Its stated training setup uses fully observed data to establish the representations that the partial-observation proxies learn to recover.
neurips-2023-offline-rl-with-discrete-pr.tldr: ORDER aligns representations from partial observations with discrete full-state representations to improve offline policy robustness.

paragraphs: Label shift occurs when class frequencies change while the distribution of inputs within each class stays the same. This paper studies adaptation as those frequencies evolve online. That invariant class-conditional distribution is central to the problem: the changing quantity is how common each class is, rather than how examples of a class are distributed.

The authors consider two settings. In the unsupervised setting, a classifier trained on offline labeled data adapts using unlabeled online observations. In the supervised setting, labeled online data must support both classifier learning and adaptation. Their algorithms reduce adaptation to online regression, building on estimates from regression procedures that track changing class proportions.

The methods guarantee optimal dynamic regret without advance knowledge of how much the label distribution will drift. This gives a theoretical characterization of performance while adapting to change. Experiments on simulated and real-world label-shift scenarios show superior performance, often with accuracy improvements of 1–3%, while remaining efficient in data and computation. The results connect a formal adaptation guarantee with practical tracking of changing class frequencies.
neurips-2023-online-label-shift-optimal-.tldr: Online regression-based algorithms adapt to changing class frequencies with optimal dynamic regret and no advance knowledge of drift.

paragraphs: Examples containing human-written rationales can improve a language model's performance during in-context learning, but producing those explanations requires substantial human effort. AMPLIFY automates rationale generation by drawing on post hoc explanation methods. These methods assign attribution scores that describe the influence of input features on a model's prediction.

The framework turns information from those attribution scores into natural-language rationales. Those rationales provide corrective signals to the language model within in-context learning. The distinctive move is to use explanations as material for improving predictions, giving them an active role in the learning process beyond describing a prediction after it has been made.

Experiments on real-world datasets report prediction-accuracy improvements of about 10–25% across a range of tasks. The gains include tasks where approaches using human-annotated rationales, such as Chain-of-Thought prompting, fall short. Additional empirical analyses and ablations examine the contribution of AMPLIFY's components. Together, the findings support automated attribution-based rationales as a promising way to improve language models while reducing reliance on manually supplied explanations.
neurips-2023-post-hoc-explanations-of-la.tldr: AMPLIFY turns post hoc feature attributions into automated rationales that improve language-model predictions in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies non-convex optimization under differential privacy, where learning must satisfy a privacy constraint while navigating an objective that can have multiple local structures. One focus is finding second-order stationary points. Building on SpiderBoost, the authors seek to improve the accuracy of gradient information used throughout optimization.

Their framework combines two gradient oracles: one estimates the gradient at a single point, while a cheaper oracle estimates the gradient difference between two points. Maintaining accurate gradient estimates through this combination improves the rates for identifying second-order stationary points. The contribution concerns how optimization obtains and reuses gradient information under privacy requirements.

The paper separately investigates global minimization using the exponential mechanism under very few assumptions. Preliminary results suggest that a regularized version can match previous empirical and population risk bounds without smoothness assumptions for polynomial-time algorithms. When running-time factors are set aside, the authors also obtain promising population risk bounds and a nearly matching lower bound. These conclusions distinguish computationally constrained results from statistical performance considered without those time factors.
neurips-2023-private-stochastic-non-conv.tldr: A two-oracle framework improves private non-convex optimization rates, while exponential-mechanism results explore global risk guarantees under weak assumptions.

paragraphs: Generating responses with large language models requires substantial computation. This paper focuses on how requests are organized during inference, using predicted response length to guide scheduling. Its central idea is to have a language model help anticipate the amount of text a request will produce before organizing requests for execution.

The proposed pipeline first predicts response lengths with minimal overhead, then groups queries with similar predicted lengths into micro-batches. This makes expected output length an explicit scheduling signal. The two stages work together: length prediction supplies information about the requests, and sequence scheduling uses that information to determine which queries should be processed together.

Evaluation on real-world instruction datasets with a LLaMA-based model reports an 86% improvement in inference throughput without reducing effectiveness. This is a result for the evaluated pipeline, expressing increased processing capacity. The authors also describe the approach as orthogonal to techniques such as FlashAttention and quantization. Its contribution can therefore complement acceleration methods operating elsewhere in the inference process.
neurips-2023-response-length-perception-.tldr: Predicting response lengths and batching similar-length queries improves inference throughput by 86% in the reported LLaMA-based evaluation.

paragraphs: Video action recognition becomes harder when parts of a scene or action are hidden. This paper studies that problem with three benchmarks and seven recognition models. Two synthetic datasets, UCF-101-O and K-400-O, allow controlled investigation of occlusion properties. A real-world dataset, UCF-101-Y-OCC, checks whether the findings extend to naturally occurring occlusions.

The experiments find that transformers are more robust than their CNN counterparts and that pretraining improves robustness to occlusion. They also reveal a gap between synthetic augmentation and real-world performance: adding occlusions during training helps, but the improvement does not generalize well to natural occlusions. This makes the real-world benchmark an important complement to controlled tests.

The authors additionally introduce CTx-Net, a simple transformer-based compositional model. In their evaluation, it generalizes well under the occlusion-related distribution shift and outperforms models trained with occlusion augmentation, especially under natural occlusions. The work supplies both a testing framework and a model result, showing why robustness should be examined across controlled and naturally occurring forms of hidden visual information.
neurips-2023-revealing-the-unseen-benchm.tldr: Three occlusion benchmarks expose robustness gaps in video recognition, while CTx-Net improves performance under natural occlusions.

paragraphs: Some neural networks use geometric spaces such as hyperbolic or orthogonal manifolds, making the geometry of optimization important. This paper extends sharpness-aware minimization, or SAM, from Euclidean space to Riemannian manifolds. The goal is to provide a sharpness-aware training framework suited to geometric models.

The resulting Riemannian SAM framework includes a new method called Lorentz SAM. It also encompasses existing variants such as Fisher SAM as special cases. This shared formulation connects methods that might otherwise appear separate and allows their behavior to be studied through a broader geometric optimization framework.

The authors provide convergence analysis using an ascent learning rate that decays less aggressively than in Euclidean SAM. Their analysis covers diverse manifolds and supplies guarantees for variants such as Fisher SAM that previously lacked convergence analyses. Experiments on knowledge graph completion and machine translation show better generalization than earlier Riemannian optimization algorithms. The contribution combines a general geometric formulation, theoretical convergence results, and empirical evidence that sharpness-aware training can benefit the evaluated geometric learning tasks.
neurips-2023-riemannian-sam-sharpness-aw.tldr: Riemannian SAM extends sharpness-aware optimization to manifolds, unifies existing variants, and improves generalization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: People observe objects and scenes changing over time, while visual foundation models commonly learn from static images. This paper asks whether video pretraining can produce representations that transfer across tasks, resist visual perturbations, and agree with human judgments. Its focus extends beyond tasks that explicitly require understanding temporal sequences.

The authors introduce VITO, combining a new video-curation procedure with contrastive learning from the complex transformations present in videos. This uses changing visual content as a source of training information. The resulting representations are evaluated on both image and video understanding, testing whether knowledge learned from video supports a broad range of visual tasks.

VITO substantially outperforms prior video pretraining methods on image tasks and image pretraining methods on video tasks. It also shows stronger robustness to natural and synthetic deformations than the compared image-, video-, and adversarially trained representations. Its predictions align closely with human judgments, exceeding models trained specifically for that purpose. These findings suggest that video pretraining could support unified, robust, and more human-aligned visual representations.
neurips-2023-self-supervised-video-pretr.tldr: VITO learns from video transformations to produce transferable visual representations with strong robustness and alignment with human judgments.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene as a collection of objects requires separating its contents while representing their spatial structure. This paper introduces sVORF, an unsupervised framework that decomposes complex scenes into individual objects from a single image. It combines object-centered representations with volumetric radiance fields to build a three-dimensional account of the scene.

A transformer first extracts object slots from the image. A hypernetwork maps those slots to volumetric object radiance fields, and the slots then guide how those fields are combined at a three-dimensional location. This connects the image's object representations with the volumetric components used to represent and render the scene.

The training procedure also uses small-sized pixel rendering to substantially reduce memory requirements. Experiments report top results for decomposition and generation on complex synthetic datasets, including Room-Diverse. Results on LLFF additionally demonstrate potential for object segmentation in real-world scenes. The evidence therefore combines strong synthetic-scene results with an initial indication of real-world usefulness, supporting further work on object-centered three-dimensional representation learning.
neurips-2023-slot-guided-volumetric-obje.tldr: sVORF uses object slots to construct and combine volumetric object radiance fields for unsupervised scene decomposition from a single image.

paragraphs: Human motion prediction uses past movement to forecast poses at future moments. The paper identifies two problems with treating all prediction times equally: attention to longer-term forecasts can hinder learning shorter-term forecasts, and information from earlier predictions is not fully carried into subsequent ones. Both problems concern how learning is organized across time.

Temporal Continual Learning, or TCL, addresses these issues through a multi-stage training framework. The authors introduce a Prior Compensation Factor to compensate during training for prior information that would otherwise be lost. They also theoretically derive a revised optimization objective, connecting the training strategy to an explicit treatment of information preservation.

The framework can be integrated with different motion-prediction backbones and adapted across datasets and applications. Experiments on four human-motion prediction benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness and flexibility. The contribution is therefore a training framework that can accompany different prediction models. It highlights the value of organizing learning across forecast times and compensating for lost prior information when building later predictions.
neurips-2023-temporal-continual-learning.tldr: TCL uses multi-stage training and prior compensation to improve human motion prediction across different forecast times and model backbones.

paragraphs: TrojLLM examines whether malicious behavior can be embedded in text prompts used with language-model services. The paper presents an automated black-box framework that discovers triggers capable of manipulating outputs when included in input data. Its setting relies on querying model APIs, making the study relevant to models accessed as external services.

The framework contains a trigger-discovery component that uses few-shot samples to find triggers applicable across varied inputs. It also includes progressive Trojan poisoning to create compromised discrete prompts that retain attack effectiveness and transferability across models. These components jointly address finding a trigger and incorporating malicious behavior into the prompting setup.

Experiments demonstrate prompt-based Trojan attacks against real-world APIs, including GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, while preserving strong performance on clean test sets. This coexistence matters: good results on clean inputs can accompany vulnerability to triggered behavior. The paper highlights security risks in prompt-based model use and mentions a potential defensive approach. Its reported findings establish the attack's feasibility in the evaluated black-box settings.
neurips-2023-trojllm-a-black-box-trojan-.tldr: TrojLLM demonstrates black-box prompt Trojans that manipulate triggered outputs while preserving strong performance on clean inputs.

paragraphs: Diffusion models with strong perceptual quality often use training objectives that look different from maximum likelihood or the evidence lower bound, known as the ELBO. This paper establishes a mathematical connection between those objectives. It shows that commonly used diffusion losses can be expressed as weighted integrals of ELBOs across noise levels.

Different training objectives correspond to different choices of weighting. Under a monotonic-weighting condition, the interpretation becomes stronger: the objective equals an ELBO combined with Gaussian-noise data augmentation. The authors show that several state-of-the-art diffusion models satisfy this condition. Monotonic weighting is a sufficient condition for this closer connection in the result presented.

The authors then investigate new monotonic weightings experimentally and achieve state-of-the-art FID scores on high-resolution ImageNet. This links the theoretical interpretation to the design of effective training objectives. The contribution helps explain why perceptually successful diffusion losses remain connected to likelihood-based learning, while providing a principled family of weightings to explore for improved image generation.
neurips-2023-understanding-diffusion-obj.tldr: Common diffusion objectives are weighted ELBO integrals, and monotonic weighting yields an ELBO interpretation with Gaussian-noise augmentation.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields reconstruct scenes from multiple images and generate views from new perspectives. A computational bottleneck is repeatedly evaluating a color network at points along each viewing ray. Geometry-guided methods reduce the number of these evaluations, but still require many calls to produce a pixel.

This paper revisits volume feature rendering, which combines the queried feature vectors along a ray before applying the color network. The combined vector is transformed directly into the final pixel color. This changes the order of computation and reduces the required color-network evaluations to one per pixel, lowering a major source of rendering cost.

The saved computation allows a comparatively larger color network to improve rendering quality while maintaining the same training and rendering time costs. The authors report state-of-the-art rendering quality on synthetic and real-world datasets with less training time than existing methods. The key contribution is a change in where feature aggregation occurs, turning fewer network calls into an opportunity for both faster reconstruction and stronger image quality.
neurips-2023-volume-feature-rendering-fo.tldr: Aggregating ray features before color prediction reduces NeRF rendering to one color-network evaluation per pixel and improves the quality–time tradeoff.

paragraphs: Offline inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer rewards and environment dynamics from a fixed set of expert demonstrations. These two estimates are closely linked: interpreting why an expert chose an action depends on what consequences the expert expected. With finite data and limited coverage, errors in the learned world model can therefore distort inferred rewards.

The paper addresses this dependency through a two-level optimization problem. The upper level maximizes the likelihood of the demonstrations using a policy model defined at the lower level. That policy model is conservative: it maximizes reward while paying a penalty that grows with uncertainty in the estimated environment dynamics.

The authors provide an algorithmic framework for solving this formulation, together with statistical and computational guarantees for the associated optimal reward estimator. Experiments on MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and D4RL datasets show large improvements over state-of-the-art offline inverse reinforcement learning and imitation-learning benchmarks. The central idea is to make uncertainty about the world directly influence the policy model used to infer the expert's preferences.
neurips-2023-when-demonstrations-meet-ge.tldr: A two-level likelihood framework uses uncertainty-penalized policy modeling to improve reward inference from fixed expert demonstrations.

paragraphs: ZipLM compresses language models around explicit runtime goals in a specified inference environment. Given a model, dataset, environment, and speedup targets, it repeatedly identifies components with the least favorable relationship between loss and runtime and removes them. This ties structural pruning directly to the deployment behavior the compressed model must achieve.

The method supports both post-training and gradual compression, as well as encoder and decoder model families. The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy–speedup tradeoffs while meeting target inference specifications. They also report lower compression costs than prior distillation and pruning techniques, making it practical to produce a family of models for different speed requirements.

The reported comparisons include outperforming prior BERT-base compression methods and matching MobileBERT's performance by pruning BERT-large. For GPT2, ZipLM outperforms DistilGPT2 while producing a model that is 60% smaller and 30% faster. These findings illustrate the value of evaluating component removal through both predictive loss and runtime in the intended environment, rather than treating model size as the sole compression objective.
neurips-2023-ziplm-inference-aware-struc.tldr: ZipLM removes language-model components according to their loss–runtime tradeoff to meet explicit inference speedup targets.
